words.etymon: dyew- (not listed by the slab mapping)
*dyew- + *ph₂tḗr (vocative compound; in the passage's context line, not word-listed)

cognate: Ved. dyauṣ (pitā) ~ Lat. Iou-/Iu-piter < *dyēws, *dyew-; Ved. pitā ~ Lat. -piter < *ph₂tḗr
drift_or_renewal: Latin has fused the vocative phrase *dyew ph₂ter into one theonym (Iūpiter), with oblique cases built on the bare stem (Iovi); Vedic keeps the two words free (dyauṣ ... pitā), separated by the clitic te/tvā
shared_syntax: theonym *dyēws + apposed *ph₂tḗr, the god named as 'Sky Father' in a direct ritual address / blessing
context: both are ritual speech to the Sky god: AV long-life charm (dyauṣ te pitā pṛthivī mātā jarāṃ mṛtyuṃ kṛṇutām 'Father Sky, Mother Earth make old age your death') and Cato's prescribed prayer at the dapes offering for the oxen ('Iupiter dapalis, quod tibi fieri oportet ... macte ... esto'), where Cato also uses the parallel 'Iane pater'. The pairing of the sky god with the kin term 'father' in a petition is the textbook Indo-European theonym formula (Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ 32x in Homer); it is not generic, since neither the deified sky nor the kin title follow from the semantics of praying
phrase: *dyēus ph₂tēr 'Sky Father' (Ved. dyauṣ pitā ~ Lat. Iupiter)

words.etymon: mer- (slab mapping; the text has a-mṛtān = amṛtān, *n̥mr̥tós)

cognate: Ved. a-mṛ́ta- ~ Gk ἄμβροτος < *n̥-mr̥-tó- 'immortal' (of gods); Ved. mártya- ~ Gk βροτός < *mr̥-tó- / *mor-tyo- 'mortal' = 'man'
drift_or_renewal: Greek has renewed the word for god (θεός for *deywó-, Ved. devá-) and in the antithesis mostly the immortal pole (ἀθάνατος beside inherited ἄμβροτος); the Plato anchor (quoting Aeschylus) keeps only the mortal pole βροτοῖς opposite θεός. Vedic keeps both cognate poles
shared_syntax: polar opposition god(s)/immortal vs. man as 'mortal', the two poles juxtaposed in one clause (Ved. devān amṛtān martyaḥ san 'I, a mortal, call on the immortal gods'; amartyā martyān 'immortals, (accompany) us mortals'; Gk θεὸς ... βροτοῖς; Hom. θεὸς ἄμβροτος ... βροτούς)
context: in both a mortal speaker or mortals as a class set against divine agents: the AV invocations ask the immortal gods to come to/aid mortals; the Aeschylean line quoted by Plato says god plants guilt in mortals. The choice of a 'death' word (*mer-) as the ordinary term for 'human' and its negation as the defining epithet of gods is a specific lexical figure shared by Indo-Iranian and Greek, not a necessity of the idea

cognate: Ved. amṛ́ta- ~ Gk ἄμβροτος (ἀμβροσία) < *n̥-mr̥-tó-; Ved. áśva- ~ Gk ἵππος < *h₁éḱwos
drift_or_renewal: in the Plato anchor the adjective appears as the derived noun ἀμβροσία 'immortal food' given to the gods' horses (an echo of Il. 13.35 / 5.777); Homer keeps the attributive ἵπποι ἄμβροτοι, and Greek also renews it as ἵπποι ἀθάνατοι
shared_syntax: *n̥mr̥tó- qualifying *h₁éḱwōs, nominative plural, the horses that draw a god's chariot (AV: aśvāḥ ... vahanty amṛtāḥ ... ratham)
context: divine chariot teams: in the AV the bay horses of the Sun draw his chariot across the sky; in the Phaedrus the gods' charioteers drive round the vault of heaven and feed their horses ambrosia; in Homer the horses of Achilles, divine gifts to Peleus, are ἄμβροτοι. Only one Vedic witness (RV has no amṛ́ta- + áśva- within 4 words, searched), and 'immortal' is a cheap epithet for anything divine, hence low

cognate: Ved. vṛ́ka- ~ Gk λύκος ~ OCS/ORu. вълкъ < *wĺ̥kʷos; Ved. ávi- ~ Gk ὄις ~ ORu. овьца < *h₂ówis
drift_or_renewal: Homer renews the prey as ἀρνός 'lamb' (Il. 16.352, 22.263); Slavic uses the diminutive derivative овьца
shared_syntax: wolf + sheep as predator/prey pair in a simile or proverb applied to a human who seizes or robs (Ved. avyā vṛkaḥ iva saṃrabhya jigīvān 'like a wolf having seized the ewe, victorious'; ORu. аще сѧ въвадить волкъ в овцѣ, то выносить все стадо 'if a wolf takes to the sheep he carries off the whole flock'); Greek proverbial ὄιν ἐν λύκοισι, λύκος οἶν ὑμεναιοῖ
context: proverbial/simile register in all three: the AV gambling charms (the winner tears his stake as a wolf the sheep, AVŚ 7.50.10), the Drevlyane proverb about Igor's extortion in the Primary Chronicle, Greek oracle/proverb language. The predator-prey image is natural to any herding culture, so the match may be independent; I report it only because the same two inherited nouns carry it in Vedic, Greek and Slavic
